text:
maria: Heads-up — canary 22 shows a weird latency spike on short prompts. 99th latency and p95 tokens/sec both regressed after the quantization change. Want an nsys run that highlights per-kernel timeline + osrt sampling and shows KV cache evictions. Any recommended CLI flags?

aaron: For short-lived stuff I usually do bracketed captures + NVTX markers. Example I run locally:```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=interval:100us --duration=20s -o /tmp/perf_run
```
Start the capture, issue the request sequence, then stop. Use --sample=interval to bias toward short kernels. Also try --capture-range=process:<pid> to reduce unrelated system noise. :thumbsup:

jen: Add NVTX ranges around kv_cache.lookup / kv_cache.evict in the runtime so the timeline can correlate samples to hits vs misses. If you can't instrument the binary, wrap the harness with NVTX pushes around the request boundary. NVTX + osrt is super helpful to see scheduling gaps.

maria: How long should I sample? The spike is intermittent ~30-90s on load tests.

aaron: Start with 20-30s and repeat the run >=5 times. Short windows bias toward long kernels; transient kernels need more repeats or bracketed sampling across many requests. If the spike triggers randomly, use a looped harness that runs requests every 5s while you capture for 30s to increase hit probability.

jen: Another trick: run a couple passes with different trace sets — one with --trace=osrt only to inspect host/device scheduling and one with --trace=cuda,nvtx to get kernel timelines. OSRT will reveal if there's a micro-spin on the host thread before kernel launch.

maria: Ran a couple captures. Preliminary notes: I see a hot kernel called "multi_head_attention_v2" that alternates with a fallback kernel depending on seq length. On KV-heavy traces there's an uptick in tiny memcpy kernels and more frequent small kernels right after what looks like kv_evict.

aaron: Sounds like the kernel selector threshold changed (seq length boundary). Check the qdrep kernel list — it includes grid/block dims and the runtime occupancy. In Nsight UI filter by kernel name and sort by cumulative time to spot which variant is costing us.

jen: For kv evict pathology, look for a pattern: kv_evict NVTX range => cluster of cudaMemcpyAsync/cudaMemcpy calls => many tiny kernels. That pattern means we might be doing eager per-shard evictions instead of batching. We solved a similar case by batching evicts and deferring prefetches.

maria: Nice. Plan: run bracketed 20s captures with NVTX around request start/finish, collect 5 qdreps, and upload to #perf for triage. If repeatable I'll open a perf regression with kernel stack + kernel-selection evidence.

perf-bot: Upload complete: s3://redwood-perf/1766612345/1766612345_run1.qdrep (attached) :file_folder:

maria: Thanks — I'll drop the qdreps and a short timeline screenshot in the perf thread. If anyone wants raw capture flags I can paste the exact command and env.

aaron: Please include the runtime NVTX commit hash and a small repro script. That helped us root the last regression quickly.

jen: Also save a short perfetto export for the host timeline if you can (nsys export --format=traced). Host-side stacks sometimes tell the real story.

maria: Will do. Appreciated!
